title: Value Semantics vs Reference Semantics
learningObjectives: Explain value semantics as using an independent value and reference semantics as access through a reference to data.
Predict how assignment and mutation may affect two variables under value or reference behavior.
Recognize copying, sharing, and aliasing as separate concepts.
Identify when shared data can create unintended side effects.
Check the language's specific rules for values, references, and copying.

understand.concept: With value semantics, assigning or passing a value generally behaves as an independent value according to the type's rules. With reference semantics, variables may refer to the same underlying object or storage, so a change through one reference can be visible through another. The terms describe behavior, not simply whether a variable is called an object.
understand.whyItMatters: Assignment and function calls can create copies or shared access. Understanding this distinction helps predict changes, avoid accidental shared-state bugs, and choose when a copy or immutable structure is safer.
understand.analogy: Giving someone a photocopy of a document is like making an independent value copy. Giving two people the same shared document link is like sharing a reference—edits by one may be visible to the other.
understand.analogyLimit: Language and type rules vary. Some types have value semantics while others are reference-based, and some languages use copy-on-write or move semantics. The analogy is not a substitute for those rules.

explain.narrative: When two variables are assigned, ask whether the assignment duplicates the relevant data or creates another way to reach the same data. Mutating shared data can affect every alias. Reassigning one variable, however, may change only that variable's binding. These two actions must be distinguished. Copying may be shallow or deep, and copying a structure that contains references can still leave nested data shared. If independence matters, use the appropriate copy operation or design immutable data.

examples.title: Independent primitive values
examples.code: let first = 4; let second = first; second = 9;
examples.explanation: Assigning the primitive value and then rebinding second leaves first unchanged in JavaScript.

examples.title: Shared object reference
examples.code: const original = {score: 1}; const alias = original; alias.score = 5;
examples.explanation: Both names reach the same object; mutating through alias is observable through original.

examples.title: Rebinding does not mutate the shared object
examples.code: let a = {value: 2}; let b = a; b = {value: 7};
examples.explanation: b now refers to a new object; a still refers to the earlier object.

examples.title: Shallow copy caveat
examples.expectedOutput: Outer object distinct; nested sharing possible
examples.explanation: A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but nested objects may still be shared unless copied separately.

examples.title: Function receives a reference-like value
examples.explanation: In JavaScript, passing an object value copies the reference value, so the function can mutate the referenced object; reassigning the parameter alone does not rebind the caller's variable.

commonMistakes: Assuming assignment always duplicates the complete structure.
Assuming a shallow copy makes every nested value independent.
Ignoring shared aliases that may be changed by another function.
Applying reference/value terminology without checking the language's exact semantics.
